title: CEO Interview with Ohad Agami of Hiveware - Semiwiki
gist: Hiveware, a Tel Aviv-based EDA startup founded in 2023 by CEO Ohad Agami and CTO Yaniv Pascal, has raised $24M to build HiveSim, a from-scratch SystemVerilog simulator claiming 5-10x single-core and 100x+ multicore speedups on ordinary CPUs, aiming to claw back full-chip verification workloads that chipmakers have pushed onto costly emulation hardware.

insights.claim: Hiveware was founded in 2023 in Tel Aviv by CEO Ohad Agami and CTO Yaniv Pascal specifically to attack the simulation runtime bottleneck in chip verification, and has raised $24M while building a team of roughly 30 engineers around that single problem.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A well-capitalized, narrowly focused EDA startup with a 30-person team signals real execution intent in simulation acceleration; watch for follow-on funding rounds or incumbent acquisition interest.
insights.quote: We raised a $24M and built a team of roughly 30 engineers focused on a single problem, simulation acceleration.

insights.claim: Ohad Agami's engineering background spans the AI chip company Hailo and Israel's Unit 81, giving Hiveware's founding team a systems-architecture and complex-verification pedigree drawn from both commercial AI silicon and an elite military tech unit.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Founder pedigree from Unit 81/Hailo is a common credibility marker among strong Israeli deep-tech startups, useful context when assessing execution risk.

insights.claim: Digital simulation performance has stayed essentially flat for three decades even as SoC complexity grew from millions of gates to hundreds of billions, creating a widening structural gap between chip design scale and the verification tools meant to check it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A tool-versus-design-complexity gap this large implies structural, multi-year demand for any verification technology that can meaningfully close it.
insights.quote: digital simulation performance has been essentially flat for three decades while SoC complexity grew from millions of gates to hundreds of billions.

insights.claim: Verification sits on the critical path to chip tape-out, and full-chip or cluster-level regressions now stretch from overnight into days or weeks, pushing engineer debug work outside normal working hours.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Longer verification cycles are a direct lever on chip program schedule and cost overruns, making verification runtime a program-level risk, not just an engineering annoyance.

insights.claim: Even well-run chip verification teams operate their compute fleets at under 40% utilization, meaning companies pay for large compute capacity that sits mostly idle because legacy simulators cannot scale across it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This implies a latent cost-saving and capacity opportunity for any simulator that can better parallelize across existing hardware, rather than requiring new compute spend.
insights.quote: even well-run teams run their compute fleets at under 40% utilization.

insights.claim: The industry's standard workaround for slow simulation is pushing workloads onto hardware emulation platforms like Palladium, ZeBu, and Veloce, trading millions of dollars and constrained emulator capacity/queue time for speed while sacrificing signal observability and debug depth.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Emulation vendors currently capture spend that could shift back to software simulation if a materially faster simulator emerges — a signal to watch in emulation hardware demand trends.

insights.claim: HiveSim is a SystemVerilog simulator built from scratch for multicore, cloud-scale compute rather than patched onto a legacy 30-year-old architecture, and runs as pure software with no GPUs, emulation, or specialized hardware required.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A clean-slate, software-only architecture is the core bet underlying Hiveware's performance and cost claims versus hardware-dependent emulation approaches.

insights.claim: HiveSim claims roughly 5-10x speedup on a single CPU core and targets more than 100x with multicore scaling (design-dependent), running entirely on the CPU infrastructure customers already own.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: If validated on real workloads, a claim this large would collapse multi-day simulation runs back into the working day — a material productivity claim worth diligencing against reference customers.
insights.quote: HiveSim delivers roughly 5-10x on a single core and aims to more than 100x with multicore, design dependent, on the CPU infrastructure teams already own.

insights.claim: HiveSim's best-fit use cases are large, long-running full-chip and cluster-level verification jobs — large AI accelerators, big CPU/GPU SoCs, mobile, and automotive designs — where the design plus testbench no longer fits an overnight simulation window.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This defines Hiveware's addressable market as large-die, high-complexity chip programs, aligning with rising verification demand from the AI silicon build-out.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: Because HiveSim is software-only simulation rather than emulation, customers keep full signal visibility and flexible debug capability that is typically lost when workloads are forced onto emulators, and it integrates directly into existing SystemVerilog/UVM flows without requiring testbench rewrites.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Retaining debug depth plus low switching cost (no rewrite) reduces adoption friction for conservative enterprise semiconductor engineering teams, easing sales cycles.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: The simulation market incumbents are Synopsys VCS, Cadence Xcelium, and Siemens Questa, alongside emulation and prototyping platforms Palladium, ZeBu, and Veloce; Hiveware's CEO argues these tools are mature but carry decades of architectural baggage never designed for today's core counts.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: A direct architectural challenge to the big-three EDA incumbents' simulation products — worth tracking whether Synopsys/Cadence/Siemens respond with parallel-native rearchitecture or acquisition of challengers like Hiveware.
insights.quote: Those simulators are mature and capable, but they carry decades of architectural baggage and were never designed for today's core counts.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like and how do you differentiate?

insights.claim: Hiveware's stated differentiation is threefold: performance on standard CPUs with no special hardware to buy, reclaiming workloads that had been pushed onto emulation while restoring full debug visibility, and dropping into customers' existing verification flows.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: Positions Hiveware as a wedge that claws back emulation-bound workloads rather than a head-on emulation or incumbent-simulator replacement, a more defensible go-to-market entry point.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like and how do you differentiate?

insights.claim: Hiveware's core technical insight is that most of a large chip design sits idle at any given simulation moment, so the biggest performance lever is eliminating computation wasted on idle logic rather than adding raw horsepower, with multicore scaling layered on top of that efficiency gain.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: This idle-logic-elimination architecture is the technical thesis underlying the 5-10x/100x speedup claims, and the key point to validate in technical diligence.
insights.quote: The biggest lever in simulation is not raw horsepower, it is wasted work.
insights.locator: What new features/technology are you working on?

insights.claim: Hiveware's roadmap centers on deeper multicore scaling and broader SystemVerilog/UVM coverage, extending the same 'compute where the design is active' principle across more of the verification flow, with the CEO describing most of the opportunity as still ahead.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: A long stated product runway suggests durability if execution holds, relevant when weighing whether current funding is sufficient to reach the next milestones.
insights.quote: The ceiling here is high, and most of the climb is still in front of us.
insights.locator: What new features/technology are you working on?

insights.claim: Hiveware's sales motion is proof-driven rather than slideware-based: engagements start with secure remote access and IT enablement, then validate performance gains directly on the customer's own production-grade full-chip or cluster-level verification workload before broader adoption.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: A benchmark-on-your-own-silicon sales approach is a credible de-risking signal for prospective customers and investors evaluating whether the performance claims hold up outside marketing materials.
insights.quote: We believe the only number that matters is the one measured on the customer's own design and testbench, so that is where we start.
insights.locator: How do customers normally engage with your company?

insights.claim: Customers' core anxieties are schedule risk from verification runtime and debug delays, the cost and queue time of emulators used to compensate, and idle compute fleets that legacy simulators cannot scale across — with the deeper fear being that tool speed and debug-cycle throughput, not design creativity, become the limiting factor on an entire chip program.
insights.speaker: Ohad Agami
insights.so_what: Frames verification tooling as a strategic, program-level bottleneck for chipmakers rather than a routine engineering nuisance, elevating simulator choice to a program-risk decision worth budget prioritization.
insights.quote: the limiting factor on the whole program is not the design team's creativity but the speed of the tools verifying their work and the number of debug cycles that can be done a day.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?
